title: Five Weeks of Walking With Poles Cut Depression Symptoms in Half, a Landmark Trial Found
excerpt: A randomized controlled trial published in the Journal of Affective Disorders found that supervised Nordic walking led to clinical remission in up to 53% of participants — offering a low-cost, stigma-free path to mental health care that could resonate in South Asian communities.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Nordic walking can halve depression symptoms in five weeks, rivaling some medications.
  • 53.6% of participants achieved full clinical remission after the trial.
  • The study involved 64 adults with moderate to severe depression.
  • Nordic walking engages 90% of the body's muscles, enhancing mood regulation.
  • Community walking groups could provide accessible mental health support in South Asian communities.

Source: Journal of Affective Disorders (2026)

Walking is the most democratic form of exercise. It requires no gym membership, no expensive equipment, and no athletic pedigree. Now, a rigorous clinical trial has shown that a specific form of walking — Nordic walking, done with specially designed poles — can halve depression symptoms in as little as five weeks, rivaling the efficacy of some pharmaceutical treatments.

The Study That Changed the Equation

Published in the *Journal of Affective Disorders* in 2026, the randomized controlled trial enrolled 64 adults with moderate to severe clinical depression. The Nordic walking group (48 participants) walked twice a week for one hour per session under supervision, while the control group (16 people) received no exercise intervention.

Using the Beck Depression Inventory-II — one of the most widely used clinical measures for depression severity — researchers tracked outcomes at baseline, five weeks, and ten weeks.

The results were striking. By the end of the program, 35 to 53.6 percent of participants in the walking group had reached full clinical remission, meaning their depression scores dropped below the diagnostic threshold entirely. Participants with severe depression actually improved faster and more dramatically during the first five weeks than those with moderate depression.

No injuries or adverse health events were reported throughout the trial.

"These findings strengthen the case for physical activity as a simple, affordable and widely accessible treatment for depression," the researchers wrote.

> ""These findings strengthen the case for physical activity as a simple, affordable and widely accessible treatment for depression," the researchers wrote."

Why Nordic Walking Works

Nordic walking engages up to 90 percent of the body's muscles — far more than regular walking — by incorporating upper-body movement through the poles. Originating in Finland as summer training for cross-country skiers, it has since become a mainstream fitness practice across Europe.

![Journal of Affective Disorders — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/8/88/Jadcover.gif)

The full-body engagement is key. Exercise triggers the release of endorphins, serotonin, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), all of which play critical roles in mood regulation. The social dimension of supervised group walking adds another layer — participants interact, share experiences, and build informal support networks, all of which are independently protective against depression.

The structured nature of the program — showing up twice a week, walking with others, being gently monitored — also gives participants a sense of routine and accountability, which depression often strips away.

The South Asian Context

Depression remains one of the most under-discussed conditions in South Asian communities. A scoping review published in *BMC Public Health* found that South Asian individuals in high-income countries face compounded barriers to mental health care: cultural stigma that frames emotional distress as personal weakness, gendered expectations around silence and endurance, and a lack of culturally competent therapists.

Benefits of Nordic Walking
›Engages 90% of body muscles.
›Triggers endorphins and serotonin release.
›Promotes social interaction and support.
›Structured program enhances routine and accountability.

"Eight out of ten participants reported that their therapist had very little understanding of the client's own cultural context," one UK study included in the review found.

For diaspora communities navigating these barriers, the appeal of the Nordic walking model is precisely that it sidesteps them. You are not "going to therapy." You are going for a walk.

Community walking groups — already a fixture in many Indian-American, British-Indian, and Indo-Canadian neighborhoods, where morning walks in parks are a social ritual — could serve as natural delivery vehicles. The Nordic walking study suggests that adding structure, moderate intensity, and some regularity to what people already enjoy could yield clinical-grade mental health benefits.

Making It Work

You do not need formal Nordic walking poles to begin. Walking sticks, trekking poles, or even starting with regular brisk walks in a group setting can capture many of the same benefits.

The study's timeline is encouraging: five weeks is enough to see meaningful change. For people who have been reluctant to explore traditional therapy — or who simply want an additional tool alongside it — this is actionable, immediate, and free.

Mental health organizations have taken note. Researchers behind the study urged policymakers to fund community exercise programs as part of mental health care infrastructure, rather than treating them solely as physical health initiatives.

Mental Health in South Asian Communities
›Cultural stigma complicates mental health discussions.
›80% reported therapists lacked cultural understanding.
›Community walking groups can bridge mental health gaps.
›Nordic walking offers a stigma-free alternative.

For South Asian communities — where silence around mental health still carries enormous weight — a walk in the park may be the most powerful first step toward healing.

Sources: Ginoux et al., *Journal of Affective Disorders* (2026), DOI: 10.1016/j.jad.2026.121618; *BMC Public Health* scoping review on South Asian mental health access; Behavioral Health News; Medical Xpress
